# control.objectives { #wdm.control.objectives }

`control.objectives`

Cost functions for the model-predictive controller.

Two objectives are offered, and the choice between them is a genuine choice
about what you want, not a tuning detail.

**Deadline.** Reach a target weight by a target date. The cost is dominated by
terminal and tracking error against a reference trajectory. If the target is
aggressive relative to what the safety constraints permit, this objective will
push against those constraints and the resulting plan will sit at the calorie
floor for weeks -- which is the controller telling you, in the only way it can,
that the deadline and the constraints are incompatible.

**Sustainable.** Lose as fast as the constraints allow, with no deadline. The
timeline becomes an output rather than an input. Usually the more honest mode,
because it surfaces the achievable date instead of quietly assuming one.

Both share the same auxiliary terms: a smoothness penalty so the plan does not
oscillate between feast and famine, and soft penalties enforcing the rate-of-loss
limit that box constraints cannot express.

## Classes

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [CostWeights](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights) | Relative weights of the cost terms. |

### CostWeights { #wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights }

```python
control.objectives.CostWeights()
```

Relative weights of the cost terms.

Units are chosen so each term is roughly O(1) at a "typical" deviation:
kilograms squared for the mass terms, and normalized calorie deviations for
the control terms. Adjusting these changes the *character* of the plan, not
merely its aggressiveness.

#### Attributes

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [carb_aversion](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.carb_aversion) | Weight on squared carbohydrate grams, per (100 g)^2. Zero by default. |
| [effort](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.effort) | Mild penalty on the squared deficit itself, per (1000 kcal)^2. |
| [progress](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.progress) | Weight on final mass in sustainable mode, per kg. Drives loss. |
| [rate_violation](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.rate_violation) | Penalty on exceeding the maximum rate of loss, per (kg/day)^2. |
| [smoothness](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.smoothness) | Penalty on day-to-day changes in prescribed intake, per (1000 kcal)^2. |
| [terminal](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.terminal) | Weight on squared terminal miss, per kg^2. Dominant in deadline mode. |
| [tracking](#wdm.control.objectives.CostWeights.tracking) | Weight on squared deviation from the reference path, per kg^2 per day. |

### carb_floor_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.carb_floor_cost }

```python
control.objectives.carb_floor_cost(carb, min_carb_g)
```

Hinge penalty on carbohydrate falling below its floor, in (100 g)^2.

### carb_preference_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.carb_preference_cost }

```python
control.objectives.carb_preference_cost(carb)
```

Sum of squared carbohydrate grams, in (100 g)^2 units.

A continuous preference for low carbohydrate, in contrast to
`carb_floor_cost`'s one-sided guard against crashing carbs to zero:
this is active at any level, not just near the floor, and grows with
``carb`` rather than only with how far below a threshold it falls.
Weighted by `CostWeights.carb_aversion`, which is zero by default,
so this contributes nothing unless deliberately turned on.

### deadline_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.deadline_cost }

```python
control.objectives.deadline_cost(
    tissue,
    reference,
    kcal,
    carb,
    fat_g,
    maintenance,
    previous_kcal,
    t_start,
    max_frac_per_day,
    weights,
    min_carb_g,
    neutral_fat_fraction,
    fat_fraction_weight,
    carb_target_fraction,
    carb_fraction_weight,
    penalty_scale,
)
```

Total cost in deadline mode.

The terminal term tracks the *reference at the end of the horizon*, not the
final goal weight. This distinction is easy to get wrong and the consequence
is severe: penalizing the gap to the ultimate target over a 28-day horizon
asks the controller to arrive within 28 days no matter how far away the
deadline actually is, and it will pin intake to the calorie floor for the
entire horizon trying. Tracking the reference instead makes the horizon a
window onto a longer plan rather than a deadline in itself.

Tracks tissue mass against the reference, not scale weight, even though the
reference itself is built from the goal's scale-weight target. Scale weight
includes the fast glycogen- and sodium-water compartments, both of which
carbohydrate and sodium intake move directly and reversibly -- so a cost
scored against scale weight can be paid down by cutting carbohydrate alone,
with zero tissue lost. Scoring tissue closes that loophole: the only way to
reduce this cost is to actually lose tissue.

``penalty_scale`` multiplies the constraint-violation terms only. The solver
escalates it until the returned solution actually satisfies the hard limits,
which is what turns these soft penalties into effective constraints.

### effort_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.effort_cost }

```python
control.objectives.effort_cost(kcal, maintenance)
```

Sum of squared energy deficits, in (1000 kcal)^2.

### macro_fraction_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.macro_fraction_cost }

```python
control.objectives.macro_fraction_cost(
    kcal,
    macro_g,
    kcal_per_g,
    target_fraction,
)
```

Squared deviation of one macro's energy share from a target, unweighted.

The "energy share" convention throughout this module is ``macro_g *
kcal_per_g / kcal`` -- e.g. fat's 9 kcal/g against carbohydrate's 4 makes
an energy-share fraction a very different number from a gram-share
fraction, and everywhere a fraction is named (``min_fat_fraction``,
``target_carb_fraction``, ...) it means the energy one.

Shared by both macros pulled toward a target -- fat via
`NEUTRAL_FAT_FRAC_WEIGHT`/`FAT_TARGET_WEIGHT`, carbohydrate
via `CARB_TARGET_WEIGHT` -- since the deviation itself is identical
in form regardless of which macro or which of the two purposes:

- **Numerical conditioning** (fat only, no stated preference): once
  carbohydrate clears its floor, nothing else in the objective
  distinguishes one fat/carb split from another (tissue dynamics do not
  depend on it), leaving a perfectly flat direction in the decision space
  that a quasi-Newton line search can fail on. Weighted small enough to
  be dominated by any term that has a real preference.
- **A real preference** (either macro, user-stated target): weighted
  large enough to actually bind, on the same footing as
  ``carb_aversion`` -- e.g. a keto-style ``target_carb_fraction`` of
  0.05-0.10 needs enough pull to hold carbohydrate down against protein's
  own, largely kcal-independent claim on the energy budget.

### rate_violation_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.rate_violation_cost }

```python
control.objectives.rate_violation_cost(tissue, t_start, max_frac_per_day)
```

Hinge penalty on daily *tissue* loss exceeding the permitted rate.

Applied to tissue mass, not scale weight, and the distinction is the whole
point. Cutting carbohydrate sharply drops a kilogram of glycogen-bound water
within days. On the scale that looks like a 4 lb/week loss and would trip any
rate limit written against scale weight -- but no tissue was lost, nothing
unsafe happened, and a controller constrained on scale weight would refuse a
perfectly reasonable plan or, worse, compensate by *raising* calories.

The limit that matters physiologically is on how fast lean and fat tissue are
mobilised. That is what this penalizes.

The limit is a fraction of each day's tissue, ``-dT_k <= frac * T_k``, so it
tightens as tissue falls, which is what "a fraction of body mass per week"
means and what `~wdm.control.mpc.check_constraints` verifies. A cap
fixed in kg/day at the starting tissue would let a long deadline plan exceed
the stated percentage in its later weeks.

One-sided: rapid *gain* is not penalized here. Uses a hinge rather than a
barrier so an infeasible starting guess still yields usable gradients.

### reference_trajectory { #wdm.control.objectives.reference_trajectory }

```python
control.objectives.reference_trajectory(
    w_start,
    w_target,
    n_days,
    days_remaining,
)
```

Linear reference path from the current weight toward the target.

Linear rather than exponential. A constant-rate path is what people actually
plan against, and it keeps the implied deficit roughly constant, which is
easier to adhere to than a front-loaded schedule.

When the horizon is shorter than the time remaining -- the usual case, since
we replan every day -- the reference covers only the horizon's share of the
total journey.

### smoothness_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.smoothness_cost }

```python
control.objectives.smoothness_cost(kcal, previous_kcal)
```

Sum of squared day-to-day changes in prescribed intake, in (1000 kcal)^2.

### sustainable_cost { #wdm.control.objectives.sustainable_cost }

```python
control.objectives.sustainable_cost(
    tissue,
    kcal,
    carb,
    fat_g,
    maintenance,
    previous_kcal,
    t_start,
    max_frac_per_day,
    weights,
    min_carb_g,
    neutral_fat_fraction,
    fat_fraction_weight,
    carb_target_fraction,
    carb_fraction_weight,
    penalty_scale,
)
```

Total cost in sustainable mode.

Linear in final tissue mass rather than quadratic: a quadratic reward for
losing would grow without bound and drive the solution straight to the
calorie floor for the entire horizon regardless of the other terms. Linear
progress traded against quadratic effort produces an interior optimum, which
is the behavior worth having.

Scored against tissue rather than scale weight for the same reason as
`deadline_cost`: scale weight is partly water, and water responds to
carbohydrate directly, so a scale-weight reward is gameable by cutting carbs
with no tissue actually lost.
